What to Do If You’re Hurt at Work: 5 Steps for Georgia Employees

Workplace injuries can happen in any industry — from construction and warehouses to restaurants, delivery work, and office environments. In Atlanta and across Georgia, many workers aren’t sure what to do after a work injury, especially when worried about medical bills, lost wages, or job security.

The Georgia workers’ compensation system exists to protect injured employees, but the steps you take immediately after a work injury matter. Failing to follow proper procedures can delay benefits — or even lead to a denied claim.

Here are five steps every injured Georgia worker should follow after a workplace injury, based on official guidance from the Georgia State Board of Workers’ Compensation.

Step 1: Report the Injury Immediately

One of the most common mistakes injured workers make is waiting too long to report the injury.

Under Georgia law, employees must report a workplace injury within 30 days of the incident to remain eligible for benefits. Reporting late can seriously jeopardize your claim.

How to report your injury

  • Notify your supervisor, manager, or HR rep
  • Provide written notice if possible (email, form, etc.)
  • Include: date, time, location, and how the injury happened

Even if the injury seems minor, report it. Many injuries worsen over time, and delays raise questions about whether the injury was actually work-related.

Learn more about your rights under Georgia Workers’ Compensation Law.

Step 2: Seek Medical Treatment from an Authorized Provider

After reporting the injury, seek medical care right away.

In Georgia, you must choose a doctor from your employer’s panel of physicians — a list of authorized medical providers. Treatment outside this list is typically not covered unless it’s an emergency.

Refer to the Georgia State Board’s Panel of Physicians Info to understand how this works.

Why this matters

  • Medical records prove your injury is work-related
  • Delays in treatment may harm your claim
  • Only authorized providers are covered by workers’ compensation

For emergencies, seek care immediately — then notify your employer as soon as possible.

Step 3: Document Everything About the Injury

Your workers’ compensation claim relies on documentation. Keeping clear records strengthens your claim and helps if legal disputes arise.

What to Document

  • Where and how the injury happened
  • Names of coworkers or witnesses
  • All medical appointments and treatments
  • Time off work and lost wages
  • Photos, prescriptions, and written doctor’s instructions

Even a simple injury log in your phone can help. This info is also vital if you later speak with an attorney from our Georgia personal injury lawyer network.

Step 4: Understand What Workers’ Compensation Covers (and What It Doesn’t)

Georgia workers’ compensation covers specific types of losses — but not everything.

What’s Covered: 

  • Medical bills for your injury
  • Partial wage replacement
  • Permanent disability or impairment benefits

What’s Not Covered:

  • Pain and suffering
  • Full salary replacement
  • Third-party injury claims (e.g., defective equipment)

In cases involving negligence by someone other than your employer — like a subcontractor or driver — you may have a personal injury claim in addition to your workers’ comp case.

Step 5: Know When to Contact a Lawyer

Not every claim needs a lawyer — but when complications arise, legal help can make a major difference.

Consult an Attorney If:

  • Your claim is denied
  • Your injury is disputed by your employer
  • Benefits stop without warning
  • You’re pressured to return to work too early
  • A third party caused or contributed to your injury

After a car accident in Atlanta, one of the first calls you’ll likely receive is from an insurance adjuster. They may sound friendly, concerned, and eager to “help you move forward.” What many people don’t realize is that insurance adjusters do not work for you—they work for the insurance company. Learn more about who we are and how we advocate for accident victims. 

In Georgia, insurance companies are allowed to protect their financial interests, even when doing so results in lower payouts to injured drivers. Understanding what insurance adjusters don’t tell you can make a critical difference in whether your accident claim is successful.

Below are the most important things insurance adjusters typically leave out—and why knowing them matters under Georgia law.

Insurance Adjusters Are Trained to Limit Compensation

Insurance adjusters are not neutral investigators. Their role is to evaluate claims in a way that limits how much the insurance company pays.

The Georgia Office of the Commissioner of Insurance (OCI)  states that it is responsible for ensuring insurers operate fairly and comply with state law—especially when it comes to how claims are handled.

What adjusters usually won’t tell you is that:

  • They are trained to look for reasons to reduce claim value.
  • Early conversations may be used to gather statements against you.
  • Quick settlements often favor the insurer, not the injured party.

Even casual comments like “I’m feeling okay” or “I didn’t see the other car” can later be used to argue that your injuries are minor or that you share fault.

You Are Not Required to Give a Recorded Statement

One of the most common tactics insurance adjusters use is requesting a recorded statement shortly after the accident. They may say it’s “routine” or “required,” but in most cases, it is not legally mandatory.

According to the Georgia OCI’s Insurance Claim Tips, policy holders should provide complete, accurate information—but you’re not legally required to give a recorded statement to the other party’s insurer unless it’s mandated by your own insurance company.

Why this matters:

  • Recorded statements can lock you into incomplete details before injuries fully appear.
  • Insurers often use inconsistencies to reduce or deny claims.
  • They may try to shift partial fault under Georgia’s comparative negligence rules.

 

Georgia’s Comparative Fault Rule Can Reduce or Deny Your Claim

Georgia follows a modified comparative negligence system. This means your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault, and if you are 50% or more at fault, you recover nothing.

While adjusters may not clearly explain this, it’s critical to understand:

  • Being 20% at fault reduces your recovery by 20%.
  • Being 49% at fault nearly cuts your compensation in half.
  • Being 50% at fault bars recovery entirely.

Adjusters may ask subtly leading questions—like whether you were distracted or could have reacted faster—to increase your share of fault and reduce what the insurer owes you.

Georgia accident attorneys understand how insurers use this tactic and can defend your version of events.
